8707.heading: Logistic Omitted Variable Bias
8707.content:
Logistic omitted variable bias occurs when an unmodeled determinant of a binary outcome alters the scale or interpretation of coefficients in the fitted model. In nonlinear models, omitted variables can affect comparisons even when they are not strongly related to the included predictors.

Measuring relevant continuous variables and avoiding unnecessary categorization can help, but an existing dataset may not contain the needed information. Odds ratios should therefore be presented as model-dependent adjusted associations rather than invariant effects.

8710.title: Logistic Model Fit Comparison
8710.heading: Logistic Model Fit Comparison
8710.content:
Logistic model fit comparison uses likelihood, deviance, degrees of freedom, or information criteria to choose between plausible specifications. A likelihood-ratio calculation is appropriate for nested models, while AIC can compare a broader set fit to the same outcome data.

The method is useful for deciding whether a predictor should be continuous or represented by category indicators. Better relative fit does not excuse post hoc searching or guarantee that the chosen representation is clinically meaningful.

8713.title: Logistic Model Deviance
8713.heading: Logistic Model Deviance
8713.content:
Logistic model deviance is a likelihood-based measure of discrepancy between a fitted logistic model and a saturated model. Residual deviance can be compared with null deviance to assess how much the predictors improve on an intercept-only specification.

Differences in deviance between nested models support likelihood-ratio comparisons when their assumptions apply. Deviance is not an absolute measure of causal quality and should be interpreted with degrees of freedom, diagnostics, and scientific plausibility.

8716.title: Logically Equivalent
8716.heading: Logically Equivalent
8716.content:
No matter what the prepositions are, we can change them and it will logically stay the same outcome or conclusion

Two formulas are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value under every permitted interpretation. Equivalence can be checked with a [[Truth Table]] or proved through a chain of [[Boolean Algebra]] laws, and it licenses replacing one formula with the other inside a larger expression.

8719.title: Logistic Model Convergence
8719.heading: Logistic Model Convergence
8719.content:
Logistic model convergence occurs when the iterative fitting algorithm reaches stable parameter estimates under its numerical criterion. Output such as the number of Fisher-scoring iterations helps show whether the calculation completed normally.

Failure to converge may reflect a badly scaled or unsupported specification, sparse categories, collinearity, or [[Complete Separation]]. A reported coefficient should not be interpreted until the cause of a convergence warning is understood.

8722.title: Logical Operators
8722.heading: Logical Operators
8722.content:
- AND
- OR
- NOT

All three of these Logical Operators can be derived from every computer program made.

AND, OR, and NOT form a functionally complete collection: any finite Boolean input-output table can be expressed using only these operators. Conditional, biconditional, and exclusive OR operators add convenient notation but can be reduced to combinations of the basic three.

8725.title: Logical Deduction
8725.heading: Logical Deduction
8725.content:
A kind of computation that can be derived from a premise and lead into a conclusion

A formal sequence of justified deductions is a proof.

More precisely, deduction preserves truth from accepted [[Premise|premises]] to a [[Conclusion]]. Rules such as [[Modus Ponens]] can be chained into a formal proof, where each line is either a premise or follows logically from earlier lines.

8728.title: Logic Bomb Malware
8728.heading: Logic Bomb Malware
8728.content:
Logic bomb malware remains dormant until a specified condition occurs. The trigger might be a date, a user action, a system state, or the absence of an expected event; after activation, the code performs its payload.

This separation between trigger and effect can make the malware difficult to notice before activation. Code review, change control, restricted privileges, integrity monitoring, and reliable backups help reduce its opportunity and impact.

8731.content:
Logic connects individual operations into a plan by determining which step follows from the current state and conditions. It supplies explicit rules for selection, repetition, and inference instead of relying on the executor’s judgment.

A logically well-formed control plan makes a computation repeatable and machine-executable. It does not establish that the premises, data, or goals are appropriate, so formal validity must be paired with domain evaluation.

8755.title: Logic and Proof
8755.heading: Logic and Proof > Chapter 1
8755.content:
"The art of logic is to find an interesting conclusion and a chain of logical deductions that leads from the premises to that conclusion." (1)

- Chapter is mostly about the mechanics of logic
- Investigating logic as a branch of math, with its own symbols, formulas, and rules of computation
A [[Proposition]] is a statement that has a truth value. It can be either true or false

[[Logical Deduction]] is a kind of computation that is derived from a [[Premise]] and can lead to a [[Conclusion]]

8756.sourceSearchName: logic and proof logic and proof
8756.title: Logic and Proof
8756.heading: Logic and Proof > Chapter 1 > 1.1 Propositional Logic
8756.content:
We use symbolic names called a [[Propositional Variable]] to talk about propositions such as p, q, and r. When we use [[Propositional Variable]]s we are discussing and agreeing on a commonly understood term for the exercise or [[Logical Deduction]] evaluation. This variable has [[Mathematical Generality]] in that p can represent any statement, and the our discussion of p will be valid, no matter which statement p represents. 

We can combine our [[Proposition]] with [[Logical Operators]] to create a new [[Proposition]]. Our new truth value is determined by our [[Logical Operators]] within our new [[Proposition]].

| English | Logical Operator | Logical Names |
| ------- | ---------------- | ------------- |
| and     | ∧                | Conjunction   |
| or      | ∨                | Disjunction   |
| not     | ¬                | Negation      |
Let:
p and q be propositions

Then:
p ∧ q
p ∨ q
¬p

Means:
p ∧ q is true when both p is true and q is true, and in no other case
p ∨ q is true when either p is true, or q is true, or both p and q are true, and in no other case.
¬p is true when p is false, and in no other case.

[[Compound Propositions]] are created from simpler [[Proposition]]s and [[Logical Operators]]

8757.sourceSearchName: logic and proof logic and proof
8757.title: Logic and Proof
8757.heading: Logic and Proof > Chapter 1 > 1.1 Propositional Logic > Precedence Rules:
8757.content:
Parentheses can be used to show which propositions are grouped together

These are in order of the highest precedence when evaluating a [[Propositional Logic]] Equation
1. Not
2. And
3. Or

Example:
¬p ∨ q ∧ r is [[Logically Equivalent]] to  (¬p) ∨ (q ∧ r)

p ∨ q ∧ q ∨ r is [[Logically Equivalent]] to p ∨ (q ∧ q) ∨ r

The chapter develops this logical foundation beyond propositional formulas through [[Predicate Logic]], quantified statements, valid inference, proof techniques, and [[Mathematical Induction]]. Its recurring theme is that discovering a useful argument can be creative even when checking each inferential step is mechanical.

8758.title: Logic and Proof

8760.heading: Logarithmic Time Complexity
8760.content:
Logarithmic time complexity, commonly written $O(\log n)$, occurs when each step reduces the remaining problem by a constant factor. Repeatedly halving a search space produces a base-two logarithm.

This growth is very slow: [[Binary Search]] can locate an item among roughly one billion ordered items in about thirty probes. Logarithmic algorithms are therefore close to [[Constant Time Complexity]] in practical scalability.

8763.heading: Log-Rank Test
8763.content:
The log-rank test compares survival curves by contrasting observed and expected events across groups over follow-up. It gives roughly equal emphasis to event times and is commonly used with Kaplan–Meier analyses.

A significant result indicates that the curves differ but does not adjust for confounders or quantify a causal effect. In R's survival-difference calculation, a weighting parameter of zero produces the log-rank form.

8766.title: Log-Normal Survival Distribution
8766.heading: Log-Normal Survival Distribution
8766.content:
The log-normal survival distribution assumes that the logarithm of event time follows a normal distribution. Its hazard can change over time, making it more flexible than the constant-hazard exponential model.

A lower AIC than an exponential fit favors it relatively, but visual agreement with Kaplan–Meier curves and scientific plausibility still matter. A good relative fit does not correct unreliable or selectively observed event times.

8769.title: Log Odds
8769.heading: Log Odds
8769.content:
Log odds are the natural logarithm of the ratio between the probability of an event and the probability of no event. Logistic regression models this unbounded quantity rather than modeling probability directly.

A logistic coefficient is an additive change in log odds, which is difficult to interpret clinically. Exponentiating it yields an [[Odds Ratio]], converting the comparison to a multiplicative scale with a no-association value of one.

8772.heading: Location-Based Mesh Component Selection
8772.content:
Location-based selection identifies vertices, edges, or faces by testing their coordinates against a bounding region. Unlike hardcoded indices, the criterion describes where the desired geometry is, making it more resilient to topology ordering and more suitable for parameterized models.

The test must define global or local space and decide how compound components qualify. A vertex can be tested directly; an edge or face may require all, any, or a representative point of its vertices to fall within the bounds. Additive selection lets several regions be accumulated before a single mesh operation.

8775.title: LOESS
8775.heading: LOESS
8775.content:
LOESS estimates a smooth relationship by fitting a low-degree polynomial to a weighted neighborhood around each target predictor value. Nearby observations receive more influence, allowing the fitted curve to follow gradual nonlinear structure without specifying one global formula.

The span controls the neighborhood size and therefore the bias-variance tradeoff. Compared with [[Bin Smoothing]], local lines or parabolas permit larger neighborhoods while retaining curvature and producing a smoother estimate.

8778.title: Location Flexibility
8778.heading: Location Flexibility
8778.content:
Location flexibility is the value gained when people can reach a computing environment and its information from different places. Network-delivered services can support remote work and global reach without keeping the application or data on one local workstation.

The benefit depends on [[Broad Network Access]], suitable client devices, identity controls, and network availability. It can improve productivity, but it also expands the locations and endpoints that must be secured.

8781.content:
A locally ringed space is a topological space equipped with a [[Sheaf]] of rings whose stalk at every point is a [[Local Ring]]. A morphism combines a continuous map with compatible sheaf maps that induce local homomorphisms on stalks.

Every [[Affine Scheme]] is a locally ringed space. The condition ensures that the sheaf records functions with a meaningful notion of value and nonvanishing near each point.

A module is locally free when its localization M_p is a free R_p-module at each relevant prime ideal p. The rank may be read from these localized free modules.

For a finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring, local freeness at every prime characterizes projectivity. This connects [[Projective Module]]s to the pointwise structure of the ring's spectrum.

An ideal is locally a complete intersection of height s when its localization at every prime containing it is generated by a [[Regular Sequence]] of length s.

A locally adaptive nearest-neighbor classifier changes its distance weighting around each test observation. Directions that separate nearby classes receive more emphasis than directions that vary without local class change.

Local adaptation can capture boundaries that a single global metric misses. It also raises computational cost because relevance or scale must be estimated during prediction, and sparse neighborhoods may not provide enough evidence for stable local weights.

A localized text map associates stable program keys with translated Unicode strings for one language. Interface code requests a key rather than embedding display text, and changing the active map switches the visible language.

Missing keys should be detectable and can fall back to a base language. The renderer must load a font containing the translated glyphs, and layouts must tolerate strings whose length differs from the source.

8796.title: Localization Universal Property
8796.heading: Localization Universal Property
8796.content:
The localization universal property says that a [[Ring Homomorphism]] R → T that sends every element of a multiplicatively closed set S to a unit factors uniquely through [[Ring Localization]] S⁻¹R.

The factor map must send r/s to the image of r multiplied by the inverse of the image of s. This property defines localization independently of a particular fraction representation.

8799.sourceSearchName: localization of quotient rings localization of quotient rings
8799.title: Localization of Quotient Rings
8799.heading: Localization of Quotient Rings
8799.content:
Localization commutes with forming a quotient. If I is an ideal of R and S maps to a multiplicatively closed set in R/I, then S⁻¹R divided by S⁻¹I is isomorphic to the localization of R/I.

This identifies two routes—first localize and then quotient, or first quotient and then localize. Both make the same denominators invertible and turn the same ideal elements into zero.

8802.heading: Localization of a Module
8802.content:
The localization S⁻¹M of an R-module M consists of fractions m/s with s in a multiplicatively closed set. It is naturally a module over the localized ring S⁻¹R.

There is a canonical isomorphism S⁻¹M ≅ S⁻¹R ⊗_R M. This identifies module localization as [[Scalar Extension for Modules]] and explains its exactness.

8805.title: Localization at an Element
8805.heading: Localization at an Element
8805.content:
Localization at an element f uses the multiplicatively closed set {1,f,f²,…}. The resulting ring R_f permits denominators that are powers of f.

Geometrically, this ring supplies functions on the basic open subset where f does not vanish. Algebraically, [[Localization as a Quotient Ring]] presents R_f by adjoining an inverse for f.

8808.content:
Localization at a [[Prime Ideal]] p uses the multiplicatively closed set R\p. The resulting ring R_p is a [[Local Ring]] whose unique maximal ideal is pR_p.

This construction studies behavior near one prime. A module or ring property is often global precisely when it holds after localizing at every prime, which motivates the notion of a [[Local Property]].

8811.heading: Localization as a Quotient Ring
8811.content:
For a ring R and element f, the localization R_f is isomorphic to R[y]/(fy−1). The new variable y represents the inverse of f, and the quotient relation forces fy to equal the [[Ring Identity]].

This presentation converts fractions into ordinary polynomial classes. It is useful when localization must be handled with ideal and polynomial computations.

8814.title: Local Outlier
8814.heading: Local Outlier
8814.content:
A local outlier is unusual relative to its immediate neighborhood even if it is not extreme with respect to the full data set. Dense and sparse regions can therefore use different effective standards.

Local methods compare a point's neighborhood density or reachability with those of nearby points. They reveal anomalies that global averages can hide.

8817.title: Local Ring
8817.heading: Local Ring
8817.content:
A local ring is a ring with exactly one [[Maximal Ideal]]. Every element outside that maximal ideal is a [[Ring Unit]], and the quotient by it is the [[Residue Field]].

Local rings focus algebra on one part of a spectrum. [[Localization at a Prime Ideal]] produces a local ring whose maximal ideal is the localized prime, making global questions accessible through pointwise analysis.

8820.title: Local Property
8820.heading: Local Property
8820.content:
A local property is a property of a ring or module that holds globally if and only if it holds after [[Localization at a Prime Ideal]] for every prime. Local checks replace one global object with a family of local objects.

Vanishing is local, and under suitable finite-presentation conditions projectivity is local. The method is powerful because each localized ring has a single relevant maximal ideal.

8823.title: Local Outlier Factor
8823.heading: Local Outlier Factor
8823.content:
Local Outlier Factor scores a point by comparing its local neighborhood density with the densities of its neighbors. A substantially lower density produces a larger indication of outlier tendency.

The method depends on the number of neighbors and distance definition. It addresses varying densities but requires many neighborhood computations.

8826.title: Local Optimum
8826.heading: Local Optimum
8826.content:
A local optimum is a solution better than all solutions reachable by one neighboring move, but not necessarily the best solution over the entire problem space. It resembles a plateau or smaller peak that appears final from the immediate surroundings.

Methods such as [[Hill Climbing]] and a [[Greedy Algorithm]] are vulnerable to this distinction because they make choices from local information. Reaching the [[Global Optimum]] may require a move that temporarily appears worse.

8829.heading: Local Optimum in K-Means
8829.content:
A local optimum in K-means is a partition that cannot be improved by the algorithm's immediate reassignment steps even though another distant partition may have lower total squared error.

Because the search follows the starting configuration, the method offers no general signal that its local solution is global. Multiple starts and comparison of final objective values are standard safeguards.

Interpretation must control for brightness, texture, saturation, and depth-dependent processing because authentic regions need not have identical apparent noise. Heavy JPEG compression and downsampling may destroy the evidence, while an informed editor can add synthetic noise to conceal a mismatch.

8835.title: Local Minimum
8835.heading: Local Minimum
8835.content:
A local minimum is a point whose objective value is no greater than values at sufficiently nearby feasible points. It describes neighborhood behavior and need not be the smallest value over the entire domain.

A differentiable interior local minimum is normally a [[Stationary Point]]. Positive curvature, expressed by a positive-definite [[Hessian Matrix]], provides a sufficient second-order condition for a strict local minimum.

8838.title: Local Maximum
8838.heading: Local Maximum
8838.content:
A local maximum is a point whose objective value is no less than values at sufficiently nearby feasible points. It may differ from the absolute maximum over the full domain.

A differentiable interior local maximum is normally a [[Stationary Point]]. A negative-definite [[Hessian Matrix]] supplies a sufficient second-order condition for a strict local maximum.

8844.content:
Local cohomology Hⁱ_I(M) is the cohomology obtained by applying [[Global Sections with Support|Γ_I]] to an injective resolution of M. It measures module behavior supported on the closed set defined by I.

The modules depend only on the radical of I and can be computed through a [[Cech Complex]]. They participate in long exact sequences, change-of-rings isomorphisms, and Mayer-Vietoris sequences.

This locality avoids brittle dependencies across distant areas of the [[System Hierarchy]]. When combined with [[Modular Behavior]], it allows distributed interactions to generate [[Emergence]] without a central script controlling the whole.

8862.title: LL(1) Parsing
8862.heading: LL(1) Parsing
8862.content:
LL(1) parsing reads input from left to right and constructs a left [[Derivation]] while using at most one lookahead symbol to select each [[Production Rule]]. It is a top-down method because it expands the start symbol toward the input string.

An LL(1) grammar must make the correct alternative identifiable from the current nonterminal and next input token. This restriction excludes some unambiguous grammars but makes predictive parsers straightforward to implement.

8865.title: Load Testing
8865.heading: Load Testing
8865.content:
Load testing sends repeated or concurrent requests to observe an application's behavior under demand. It reveals how latency and successful request rates change as work approaches the capacity of the API, database, or host.

A useful test targets a representative endpoint with a repeatable scenario. Results should be compared before and after an optimization rather than treated as an isolated score.

8868.title: Load Imbalance
8868.heading: Load Imbalance
8868.content:
Load imbalance occurs when parallel workers receive unequal amounts of useful work and some become idle while others remain busy. In graph processing, a few high-degree vertices can dominate the edges assigned to one partition.

Dynamic work queues, finer partitions, work stealing, and degree-aware distribution can improve balance, but each adds coordination or data-movement cost.

8889.heading: Lithotripsy
8889.content: Extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy breaks kidney stones with focused high-intensity pressure pulses delivered from outside the body. Repeated pulses fragment the stone into pieces small enough to pass through the urinary tract.

8892.title: Literate Programming
8892.heading: Literate Programming
8892.content:
Literate programming interleaves explanatory prose with executable code so a document describes both an analysis and how it was produced. Computed results are generated from the same instructions presented to the reader.

The approach reduces divergence between code, figures, tables, and narrative when the source document is recompiled.

8910.content:
The LINQ `Where` operator selects sequence elements that satisfy a Boolean predicate. It preserves the element type and returns a query that yields only matching values when enumerated.

Multiple filters may be chained or combined into a single predicate. With a remote provider, predicates can be translated and applied near the data source, which can greatly reduce the amount of data returned to the application.

8913.content:
`OfType<T>` filters a heterogeneous sequence to elements compatible with a requested type and returns them as that type. Incompatible values, including null values when the target requires an object of the chosen type, are omitted rather than causing a cast failure.

This differs from `Cast<T>`, which attempts to cast every element and fails when an item is incompatible. Type filtering is therefore useful when a mixed sequence is expected and only one subtype is relevant to the next stage of a query.

LINQ to XML represents XML documents with objects such as `XDocument`, `XElement`, and `XAttribute`. Standard query operators can navigate, filter, project, and group nodes while construction syntax makes new XML trees composable from ordinary expressions.

Element names, namespaces, and missing content must be handled deliberately because XML structure carries meaning beyond text values. The model is convenient when a document fits in memory; forward-only XML readers remain preferable for very large streams.

8919.heading: LINQ Set Operations
8919.content:
LINQ set operators compare sequences according to element equality. `Distinct` removes duplicates, `Union` combines unique values, `Intersect` keeps values found in both inputs, and `Except` keeps values from the first input that are absent from the second.

Correct results depend on the equality semantics of the element type or an explicitly supplied comparer. These operations describe mathematical membership, so they should not be used when duplicate counts or original ordering carry essential meaning.

8922.content:
A LINQ query provider interprets a query expression for a particular data source. In-memory sequences execute delegates through `IEnumerable<T>`, while `IQueryable<T>` providers inspect expression trees and may translate them into SQL or another remote query language.

This distinction explains why not every .NET method can be used in a database query and why execution behavior varies by source. Provider-backed queries should be evaluated for their generated operations, not assumed to behave like ordinary in-memory loops.

8925.title: LINQ Projection
8925.heading: LINQ Projection
8925.content:
Projection transforms each input element into a chosen output shape with `Select`. The result may be a single property, a calculated value, an anonymous object, a tuple, or a purpose-built data-transfer type.

Selecting only needed fields separates the consumer's view from the source entity and can reduce data transfer for provider-backed queries. Projection also marks a conceptual boundary: filtering decides which items remain, while projection decides what each remaining item becomes.

8928.title: LINQ Ordering
8928.heading: LINQ Ordering
8928.content:
LINQ orders a sequence with `OrderBy` or `OrderByDescending` and adds subordinate keys with `ThenBy` or `ThenByDescending`. Each key selector extracts the value used at that level of comparison.

Calling a new `OrderBy` starts a new primary ordering, whereas `ThenBy` preserves the existing priority. Stable, explicit ordering is essential whenever consumers depend on deterministic presentation, paging, or selection of first and last elements.

8931.title: LINQ Lambda Expression
8931.heading: LINQ Lambda Expression
8931.content:
A lambda expression is a compact anonymous function commonly supplied to LINQ operators as a predicate, selector, key function, or accumulator. Its parameters represent items flowing through the query, and its body describes the operation to apply.

The same syntax may compile to a delegate for in-memory execution or to an expression tree for provider translation. That contextual conversion is central to LINQ's ability to present one query style across very different data sources.

The inventory example passes a lambda as a product-price criterion to a filtering operation. The filtering mechanism remains unchanged while the lambda expresses the caller's selected business rule, illustrating a functional form of strategy selection.

8934.heading: LINQ Join and Group
8934.content:
LINQ joins relate items from two sequences through matching keys. `Join` produces a flat sequence of matching pairs, while `GroupJoin` associates each outer item with a sequence of matching inner items.

Grouping organizes elements by a selected key and yields groups that can be projected or aggregated. Joins and groups make relationships explicit in the query, but the shape and cost of their translation depend on whether execution is local or delegated to a provider.

8937.heading: LINQ Extension Methods
8937.content:
Language Integrated Query is built largely from extension methods such as `Where`, `Select`, and `OrderBy`. They let query operations appear as fluent members of enumerable or queryable sequences while remaining static methods defined by the LINQ libraries.

Chaining these methods forms a pipeline in which each operation receives a sequence and produces another sequence or a final scalar value. Many operators use deferred execution, so defining the query and enumerating its results are distinct events.

8940.title: LINQ Aggregation
8940.heading: LINQ Aggregation
8940.content:
Aggregation reduces a sequence to a summary value. Operators such as `Count`, `Sum`, `Average`, `Min`, and `Max` express common summaries, while `Aggregate` carries a custom accumulator across the elements.

Empty sequences and numeric types affect the behavior of an aggregate, so callers should understand each operator's return and failure rules. With a query provider, aggregation is often translated so the data source computes the result without returning every row.

8943.heading: Linked Unsupervised Feature Selection
8943.content:
Linked unsupervised feature selection couples feature choice to both local data geometry and the global cluster structure inferred from that geometry. Rather than completing selection and clustering as isolated stages, it lets each refine the other.

The link can improve consistency between representation and partition, especially when labels are absent. It also creates a nonconvex joint problem whose outcome may depend on initialization, graph construction, and the relative weight placed on selection versus clustering.

8949.title: Linked List
8949.heading: Linked List
8949.content:
A linked list is a data structure whose nodes store payload data and a [[Pointer]] to the next node. The first node is called the head, and the last node points to null to mark the end.

Items need not occupy consecutive memory locations because each pointer supplies the address of the next item. [[Linear Search]] can traverse the list by following these links, while self-organizing methods can change node order after successful searches.

8958.title: Link Sink
8958.heading: Link Sink
8958.content:
A link sink is a group of web-graph nodes with incoming links from outside but no outgoing path back to the rest of the graph. Once a path enters the group, its links keep movement trapped within the group.

In PageRank, a link sink can absorb rank even when no individual [[Dangling Node]] exists. [[PageRank Teleportation]] gives the random surfer a probability of jumping anywhere, preventing a closed group from draining importance from every other page.
